https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: Upper secondary schools will be required to monitor how computers are being used for written exams. Photograph: Posed by models; Solskin/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Upper secondary schools will be required to monitor how computers are being used for written exams. Photograph: Posed by models; Solskin/Getty Images AI (artificial intelligence) Danish pupils will have to orally defend essays in attempt to combat AI cheating Government introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19 Europe live – latest updates Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Thu 6 Aug 2026 07.58 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Danish teenagers will have to make an oral defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating, the government has announced. Pupils aged 16 to 19 at upper secondary school (known in Denmark as gymnasiet ) will also be encouraged to do written assignments at school under controlled conditions, including monitoring of their computer screens, rather than at home. The measures, announced on Thursday as pupils prepare to go back to school next week after the summer break, will come into immediate effect after Magnus Heunicke, the country’s education minister, demanded urgent action. “Unfortunately, we have a problem with AI cheating in upper secondary schools,” he said. “Action is needed now.” AI had posed a growing challenge to teaching and exams, the education ministry said. It is hoped the new measures will help to establish clearer guidelines for when pupils are not permitted to use it. The government is also preparing a comprehensive national strategy for AI use in all schools and the wider education sector. Heunicke said he would speak to schools, teachers and students to “ensure that AI does not undermine students’ competencies, professionalism and, not least, the ability to think for themselves”. The first measure to be introduced is the oral defence of exam assignments written at home. About 9,000 upper secondary school students each year write a big assignment (known as større skriftlige opgave or SSO), which they will now have to defend orally. The ministry said it would speak to schools about the best way to do this. Upper secondary schools will also be required to use monitoring tools to oversee how computers are being used for written exams. They are required to install firewalls to filter what is available on the school network during exams and teaching. The third measure is a plea to schools to encourage pupils to do more of their written assignments at school under controlled conditions, to “follow the students’ work process, provide relevant feedback and create a more accurate basis for assessment”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion The ready availability of AI tools is upending education around the world for teachers and pupils, leaving governments scrambling to assess if and how they should intervene. In neighbouring Sweden, a study found that the number of students suspended or warned for unauthorised AI use rose by 688% between 2023 and 2025. The government has commissioned a review into how schools are tackling AI cheating, which will report back in April. Announcing the review, Lotta Edholm, the Swedish minister for upper secondary school, said in January: “There is no reason to turn a blind eye to cheating students. Cheating is completely unacceptable regardless of what form. It risks affecting grades that should reflect students’ knowledge and in the long term, students are not actually learning what they should.” Explore more on these topics AI (artificial intelligence) Denmark Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Danish state could face legal action over deal that gives US powers on its soil Nato chief urges ‘thoughtful diplomacy’ after US treasury secretary’s jibe at Denmark Denmark to remove ‘pornographic’ mermaid statue, reports say Denmark rethinking 40-year nuclear power ban amid Europe-wide shift Denmark’s museum objects at risk from ‘extreme’ new mould, say conservators Nearly half of Danes see US as threat and 78% oppose Greenland sale, poll shows Danish PM says Europe must ‘stand together’ as Trump threatens Greenland On Denmark's Jutland coast an elegant new museum counters a Nazi monolith ‘I’ll sleep on dunes under the stars’: writer Ben Love on Denmark’s beautiful coast Highlights of Denmark: readers’ travel tips Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Following the announcement about Andy Burnham’s early prison release scheme to alleviate overcrowding in prisons, there has been outcry from the public. Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Following the announcement about Andy Burnham’s early prison release scheme to alleviate overcrowding in prisons, there has been outcry from the public. Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images First Edition newsletter Prisons and probation Wednesday briefing: Why the prison crisis is about much more than early release In today’s newsletter: As ministers scramble to resolve overcrowding in prisons, experts say the crisis demands a rethink of who we lock up – and what happens when they’re set free Libby Brooks Wed 12 Aug 2026 01.47 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 01.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. On his family holiday last week, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was reported to be taking daily calls from Ministry of Justice officials about his government’s early release scheme. A furious public outcry has gathered pace since it emerged that the plan – brought in by his predecessor, Keir Starmer, to alleviate overcrowding in prisons across England and Wales – might include two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper and other serious sexual offenders, including grooming gang perpetrators. After several weeks of “system says no” briefings, which Harper’s mother Debbie Adlam has described as “a rollercoaster … really draining”, yesterday Burnham endeavoured to put a pin in it until September. Announcing that he had tasked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, with fast-tracking measures to free up prison space, the prime minister insisted he was “increasingly confident” that the early release scheme can be adapted to exclude the constable’s killers. He had previously intervened to exempt grooming gang members, rapists and those convicted of “serious” child sexual offences. Norris will report to parliament early next month, and Burnham is no doubt keen that this week’s nationwide listening tour is not derailed by constant questions about early release. But the scrutiny is unlikely to recede with opposition parties calling for a U-turn and probation officers yesterday voting decisively in favour of strike action over excessive workloads – a problem they expect to get worse when the scheme starts in the autumn. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to criminal justice consultant and former repeat offender Gethin Jones , and former prison governor John Podmore , about the story missing from the early release row, and what a radical solution to the ongoing prison capacity crisis might look like. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK news | Repeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely to have cost the UK economy more than £4bn in lost economic output by the end of July, new analysis shows. Meta | Courts in England and Wales have joined a number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in banning the controversial Meta glasses , which can record video footage while being worn. Middle East | Firefighters and residents of south Lebanon have accused the Israeli military of lighting wildfires in the region, as forested areas burned down in blazes sparked by Israeli bombing. UK politics | Reform’s deputy leader Richard Tice has been accused of using “nasty tactics” in an attempt to intimidate journalists and deflect attention from his own financial affairs after issuing a legal threat to the Guardian. US news | Democrats called on Tuesday for a congressional briefing over a stunning charade in which Donald Trump was secretly spirited to a different plane than the one the public and press believed he was travelling on. In depth: ‘We should be locking up people we’re afraid of, not people we’re mad at’ View image in fullscreen HMP Manchester, known as Strangeways, struggled with overcrowding, riots and brutal conditions in the 1990s. Photograph: Phil Noble/PA Gethin Jones recalls watching a documentary about HMP Strangeways, the crumbling Victorian prison in Manchester that became synonymous with over-crowding and brutal conditions. The Strangeways riot of 1990 was a watershed moment in British penal history, leading to long-awaited public scrutiny and reform. While the echoes of those days are all too apparent, what he recalls most clearly was the then-governor describing prison as “society’s dustbin”. At that point, Jones was already set in his own 20-year cycle of drug misuse and offending: after a childhood in care, he received his first custodial sentence at the age of 14, and was introduced to heroin and crack cocaine in prison. He’s now a passionate advocate for the type of “human to human” intervention that eventually unlocked his own offending cycle – working with men in secure environments. “Politicians keep saying we lock people up to keep communities safe,” he says. “But the reality is that when you lock somebody up, if you do nothing with them while they’re in prison, and nothing to support them when they get out, they’re even more disadvantaged and more likely to reoffend, which is now making our communities unsafe.” The current row over early release is focused on a small percentage of offenders, he argues, while most of those in prison are low risk, high need. “They are people with poor mental health, substance misuse, no opportunities: all of these areas that our society doesn’t know how to manage, then they fall into the justice system and then they go into the dustbin, which is prison.” Why are our prisons at capacity? According to the most recent Ministry of Justice data , there are 86,536 men and women in prison custody in England and Wales, one of the highest per capita prison populations in western Europe. It’s a population that has doubled in recent decades – from about 44,000 in 1993 – for a number of interlocking reasons. The hefty courts backlog and wider system gridlock brought about by the pandemic has seen the remand population balloon to more than 15,000, almost 18% of the total in custody. Recalls – the term for people returned to prison after breaching the conditions of their release – have likewise increased by a staggering amount. There were 51,419 licence recalls in England and Wales in year ending March 2026, compared with 40,259 the previous year. Many experts see this as a direct consequence of previous early release schemes: without proper planning, the policy creates a revolving door. Others blame the risk aversion of an over-burdened probation service. Jones is working with a young man who is about to be released from prison for the second time, having been recalled a mere six days after a drug relapse meant he failed to report to his probation hostel in time. “He’s just about to get out now, and there’s still not the support in place. It will be an absolute miracle if he doesn’t get recalled again.” Added to this mix is the fact that judges are imposing ever-longer prison sentences – from an average of 16 months for an indictable offence to 1993 to 22.2 months in 2024. When he was asked to review sentencing by Keir Starmer, former Conservative justice secretary David Gauke attributed it to a “bidding war” between political parties since the 1990s over which can show themselves tougher on crime. And overseeing all of this is another revolving door: that of the entrance to the Ministry of Justice. In the past 10 years, there have been 10 justice secretaries and 13 prison ministers. What is the cost of early release? Regardless of sentence inflation, and unhappily for politicians, the public believe prisons are failing to punish prisoners for their offences and not preparing them adequately for a life beyond crime. What is unclear is how aware they are of the administrative sleight of hand whereby successive governments have driven up sentence lengths through legislation, then sought to undo the effect through early release schemes. Richard Garside, director of the Centre for Crime and Justice Studies, has written powerfully about the impact on individual victims: “What should not survive indefinitely is the current arrangement, in which parliament promises punishment that cannot be delivered, and the gap is closed administratively, out of sight, until a letter lands on a victim’s doormat.” In a Facebook post on Tuesday, the prime minister acknowledged “the anguish of [PC Andrew Harper’s] family and, more broadly, of all those victims and their families who may see those who caused them such harm not serve their full sentence”. But the operational impact is significant . Prison Service leaders are described as “terrified of another exemption” to early release as they cope with severe over-crowding, and must now navigate the haphazard system of sentence discounts and days added in order to determine who is eligible. Previous schemes resulted in some prisoners being released in error , while probation managers found their caseloads distended overnight. What could Andy Burnham do differently? In the same Facebook post, Burnham said these exemptions could be mitigated by expanding prison places in three ways: removing foreign offenders more quickly; tackling “the long-running injustice of IPP sentences” , which have kept many minor offenders locked up for decades; and re-purposing some women’s prisons for male offenders. Our home affairs editor Rajeev Syal assesses their viability here . John Podmore, former governor of Belmarsh, Brixton and Swaleside prisons, has argued consistently that prisons not only fail to rehabilitate, but in too many cases actively institutionalise despair. The longer-term solution to the present crisis is not, he tells me, to build more prison places – despite Burnham’s colleagues pushing this line yesterday. Podmore has always made a clear distinction between those who threaten the public – probably fewer than 30,000 of the current population, by his informed estimate – and the rest: “We should be locking up people we’re afraid of, not people who we’re mad at.” The government is pressing ahead with its aim to build 14,000 more prison places by 2031, mainly secure category B and C facilities – but a good proportion of the prisoner population is within 12 months of release. “We don’t need those levels of security,” Podmore says. “We need more open prisons in urban areas, more approved premises, more bail hostels.” Female prisoners – the vast majority of whom are nonviolent offenders – are in particular need of more creative facilities like Hope Street in Southampton, which offers a community alternative to prison for women so their children can remain with them. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion For Podmore, Burnham’s devolution agenda offers a gateway to radical prison reform: a centrally run federal estate for those who require long-term high security; and oversight of prisons for lesser offenders – who have been thoroughly risk assessed – passed to local mayors. After all, as Gethin Jones has already explained, lack of resettlement support is one of the biggest hurdles facing newly released prisoners. Aren’t local authorities better placed to bring them into existing housing, education and mental health networks? Might a truly local prison have a board of governors, like a school, making its management answerable to that community? When Podmore took over HMP Brixton in 2003, it was languishing at the bottom of performance league tables, with angry headlines demanding its closure. He opened the doors, inviting in local community charities and religious groups. “And the response was, ‘What can we do?’ That’s where you change the public perception.” What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen The first real food-influencer … Anthony Bourdain in Sydney, 2005. Photograph: Fairfax Media/Getty Images I spent half my holiday sharing a cottage with a wasp nest, and was glad to read in the latest instalment of Invertebrate of the Year that my policy of non-engagement was the correct one, definitively settling an argument with my other half. Libby Josh Halliday’s piece about Matilda Davis , a mother who took her own life after she was “pushed to breaking point” by a care system that fails the parents of so many disabled children, was a moving profile of a remarkable woman. Hettie The forecast cloud cover over Glasgow suggests that solar eclipse viewing won’t be that fruitful, but I was still happy to watch our snappy public service video about how to watch it safely. Libby Anthony Bourdain was the world’s first real food influencer who taught us all to avoid brunch like the plague. Zoe Williams spoke to chefs about whether they still admire his hedonistic vibe. Hettie ICYMI, you must make time to read this brilliant and disturbing essay from Katherine Rundell about how AI stands between children and their potential for thinking. I finished it feeling angry – but also, hopeful. Hettie Sport View image in fullscreen Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu celebrate winning gold and silver. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA European Athletics Championships | Britain’s Romell Glave won a stunning gold in the men’s 100m at the European championships, with his teammate Jeremiah Azu picking up silver. Football | England defender Djed Spence nears Tottenham Hotspurs exit , with the club allowing him to join Inter in a move expected to cost around £25.6m. Fifa | Gianni Infantino’s opponents are working together to produce a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as a system of patronage that Fifa has adopted since he replaced Sepp Blatter as president 10 years ago. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “Burnham plan to keep PC’s killers in jail could backfire, warn unions”, is the Guardian ’s front page today. The Telegraph says “Police unite to fight early release”, the Express has “Andy U-turns on early release plan”, and the Times writes “Extra safeguards needed for early release, say police”. The FT has “European car industry wary as China tightens grip on component suppliers”, the i Paper has “Summer 2026 will be UK’s hottest since records began”, and the Mail writes “Burnham” Middle-class areas must take more migrants”. Lastly, Metro leads on “The Black Wednesday shopping scramble!”. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen Farage says he’s protesting against the scrutiny into his financial affairs – and that the people of Clacton should decide whether he’s still fit to serve. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Could Clacton bin off Nigel Farage? Nigel Farage has taken a high risk gamble by resigning and forcing a byelection in his constituency. Nosheen Iqbal heads to Clacton to find out how voters feel. Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nicola Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Umit, a wild-caught female tiger, is released into Kazakhstan’s wilderness as part of a repopulation programme. Photograph: Amur Tiger Centre/TASS/Zuma Press/eyevine Caspian tigers were last sighted in Kazakhstan more than 70 years ago. Earlier this month, a female Amur tiger, a breed whose DNA is virtually identical to Caspians, was released into a nature reserve in Kazakhstan as part of a pioneering repopulation programme. “ Umit ,” which translates to “hope” in Kazakh, was transported to the reserve from the far east of Russia, and soon, she will be joined by more big cats. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken,” said Kazakhstan’s environment minister. Photograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Police officers escort Phra Wachirayan Wi outside the Central Investigation Bureau in Bangkok on Thursday. Photograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/AFP/Getty Images Thailand Buddhist monk arrested in Thailand on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m Phra Wachirayan Wi arrested alongside woman he was filmed having sex with in latest scandal to hit country’s clergy Agence France-Press in Bangkok Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police in Thailand have arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with. The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in the Buddhist-majority country, after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances. Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century temple Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, according to the lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan. A 47-year-old woman accused of helping convert and conceal the money was also arrested. Leaked CCTV footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media. In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions. Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in mid-July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds. Pattanasak, a commander of the police crime suppression division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name. About 89m baht ($2.7m or £2m) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8m baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said. “But the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account – not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference on Friday. View image in fullscreen Police say authorities seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg of gold bars, jewellery, watches and land title deeds Photograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/Thai News Pix/AFP/Getty Images He said authorities had seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg (35lb) of gold bars and jewellery and 28 land title deeds. Police are investigating which are personal property and which belong to the temple. “We will expand the investigation to identify other people involved and restore public confidence in Buddhism ,” said Nattasak Chaowanasai, the commissioner of Thailand’s Central Investigation Bureau. Wat Phutthaisawan is a prominent royal monastery with a large following that includes government officials, businesspeople, police and military personnel. The former abbot, also known as Luang Pho Atichot, was well known for making amulets, with the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, reported to be among those who wore his creations. The abbot was defrocked shortly after his arrest. Last year, police arrested a woman accused of blackmailing at least 11 monks she had sex with , extorting nearly $12m of monastery funds from them, in a case that shook Thailand. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz6.text: Image source, Getty Images By Hafsa Khalil Published 51 minutes ago US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks. "It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House. Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown. Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon. The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries. Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US. Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks. "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday. Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin". But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart. Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down". Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible. In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict. On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network. Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks. A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network. "Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read. On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine. Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine. Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda. The war will cost â¬155bn (Â£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least â¬70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons. Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid.
